parties:
Belayet Hossain (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Shah Alam Parvez and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the order dated 24-4-97 passed by the 3rd Court of Additional District Judge, Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 1996 affirming the order dated 13-4-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Dinajpur rejecting an application for local investigation at the instance of the pre-emptee. 

 2. Short facts relevant for the purpose, of the case are that the petitioner as pre-emptor filed a pre-emption case in the Second Court of Munsif at Dinajpur, being Miscellaneous Case No. 99 of 1970, which was subsequently renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 83 of 1984, praying for pre-emption of the case property under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The pre-emptor''s case, in short, is that, he is a co-sharer by purchase in respect of the case land while the pre-emptee is a stranger thereto. It has been alleged that by the registered kabala dated 26-12-69 opposite party Nos. 2-5 sold the case land to the pre-emptee without serving any notice upon him. Soon after coming to learn about the disputed sale, the pre-emptor promptly filed the case for pre-emption on fulfilling all the legal requirements. 

 3. Pre-emtpee opposite party No.1 contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations of the pre-emption application and contended, inter alia, that the pre-emption case is not maintainable in law and the pre-emptor has no locus, standi to maintain the pre-emption case. It has also been contended that the petitioner is not a co-sharer in the case land. It was further contended that after the purchase, the pre-emptee made improvement in the case property by spending a huge amount of money and, if pre-emption is allowed, he is entitled to improvement costs. 

 4. The learned Munsif by his impugned judgment dated 31-12-73 disallowed pre-emption on contest. Being aggrieved the pre-emptor-petitioner took an appeal before the District Judge, Dinajpur being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 23 of 1974 and the learned Appellate Court was ultimately pleased by its judgment dated 30-3-75 to allow the appeal on seting aside the judgment and order of the trial Court and sent back the case on remand to the trial Court for a fresh trial. Against the aforesaid order of remand the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 preferred Civil Revisional No.805 of 1975 before this Court and this Court by its judgments dated 21-8-95 discharged the Rule and maintained the order of the Court of appeal below. Eventually, the case was transferred to the Court of the Munsif at Sadar Dinajpur and it was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 83 of 1984. At this stage the pre-emptee filed an additional written objection on 20-1-96 claiming improvement cost to the tune of Taka 27,120.00 for developing the case property and thereafter filed another application for local investigation for ascertaining the real cost of improvement and the learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 16-6-86 kept this application with the record for considering it at the time of hearing of the case, with option to the pre-emtpor to raise objection against the maintainability of the application for ascertaining development cost by a commissioner. By this order, the learned Assistant Judge also found that improvement cost can be determined only by the Court on taking evidence. Against the aforesaid order, the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.68 of 86 before the District Judge, Dinajpur and the said appeal was subsequently dismissed by Judgment and order dated 29-10-91. Against the aforesaid judgment and order dated 29-10-91 the pre-emptee opposite party preferred Civil Revision No. 2267 of 1992 before this Court and eventually this Court by its judgment and order dated 21-8-95 discharged the Rule and directed the learned Assistant Judge to dispose of the ancient pre-emption case within a period of two months. The certified copy of the judgment of the aforesaid revision case has been annexed to this petition and marked as Annexure-C thereto. Thereafter the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 once again filed additional written objection alleging, inter alia, that during the pendency of the Civil Revision he made further development in the suit property by spending Taka 1,40,000.00 and the pre-emptor is liable to pay the said improvement cost with interest accrued thereon. Thereafter on 6-4-96 the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 filed an application for local investigation for ascertaining the actual improvement incurred by him at the second and third phases and the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned order dated 13-4-96 allowed the said prayer. Being aggrieved, the pre-emptor took an appeal before the District Judge, Dinajpur being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 1996 and the learned 3rd Court of Additional District Judge, who heard the appeal, has been pleased by the impugned order dated 24-5-97 to dismiss the appeal, affirming the order of the trial Court. It is against that order the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. Mr Enayetur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that in the face of the order dated 16-6-86 made by the learned Asstt. Judge himself Annexure 'B' to the petition and in the face of the clear direction by this Court for disposal of the three-decade old pre-emption case within a period of two months, the learned courts below evidently erred in law in passing the impugned order on a completely erroneous view of law regarding the provisions of Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Rahim further submits that having regard to the provision of section 23(3) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy, Act 1949 there is no scope for awarding any cost of improvement made after getting notice of the case and, as such, the learned Courts below erred in law in passing the impugned orders illegally and arbitrarily. The learned Advocate also submits that the alleged cost of improvement, if at all permissible in law, can be determined only by the learned Court by taking evidence and that cannot be left to be decided by an Advocate Commissioner and consequently, the learned Courts below erred in law in passing the impugned orders illegally on a casual view of the matter allowing unwanted bounty, to the pre-emptee to delay the disposal of the pre-emption case for unlimited period. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has placed before me the impugned order. It is an undisputed fact that the pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 has been making demand for improvement costs by phases. Section 24(3) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 appears to be a prima facie bar against his claim for improvement cost for any improvement made after receiving notice of the pre-emption case. He can succeed in his claim only when he satisfactorily proves that he made the alleged improvement bonafide for the beneficial development of the case property. All these are matters for the trial Court to decide on taking evidence and these cannot be left to the Commissioner for his determination. The learned Additional District Judge in his impugned order clearly found that the alleged development costs can be determined only by the Court itself on taking evidence while local inspection may simply provide some additional materials for proper determination of the quantum of development costs, whenever found necessary under given circumstances. 

 8. Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for holding local investigation on specified grounds when the Court finds a local investigation necessary and proper for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute but the Court has no power to delegate its authority to the Commissioner for ascertaining facts which are required to be decided by him alone on taking evidence. In the instant case, the trial Court will first have to decide as to whether the pre-emptee is entitled to the alleged development costs. If the Court finds the answer in the affirmative, then and then only the question of determination of the quantum of development cost will arise. In the facts and circumstances of the case, I do not find any necessity nor any scope to order for holding local investigation of the case land for deciding the question of improvement costs allegedly incurred by the pre-emptee opposite party at different stages of the case. The learned courts below appear to be oblivious of the scope of Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the provision of section 34(3) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, and allowed themselves to be led by illegal and irrelevant considerations. From the facts and circumstances of the case, it is evident that the pre-emptee opposite party is out to delay the disposal of the case by any means and in the process he has successfully consumed about 25 years in forestalling the disposal of the pre-emption case. It is unfortunate that even the order of this Court for disposal of the pre-emption case positively within two months passed in Civil Revision No. 2267 of 1992 by Judgment dated 21-8-95 has failed to produce any impact upon the learned Assistant Judge and he indulged in the luxury of flouting the order of this Court on illegal, irrelevant and fanciful considerations. The learned trial Court must remember that any order passed by a superior Court is binding upon it and any act of negligence in complying with it tantamount to disobedience, entailing legal consequences. 

 10. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned order dated 24-5-97 passed by the learned 3rd Court of Additional District Judge, Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 1996 affirming the order dated 13-4-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Case No.83 of 1994 allowing an application for local investigation is set aside. 

 13. In view of the fact that the pre-emption case is more than 25 years old, it is absolutely necessary in the interest of justice that it be disposed of with utmost expediency. The learned Assistant Judge, Sadar Dinajpur is hereby directed to dispose of Miscellaneous Case No.83 of 1984 within six weeks from the date of receipt of the order of this Court and to report compliance without fail.
